title: Review: Membranes and membrane transport; Organelles and compartmentalization; Cell specialization

Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Integral protein
items.clue: A membrane protein that is embedded in the lipid bilayer, in one of the two lipid layers or spanning both.

items.label: Aquaporin
items.clue: An integral membrane channel protein with a narrow pore that allows water molecules, but not ions or other solutes, to pass through.

items.label: Facilitated diffusion
items.clue: The passive movement of particles across a membrane, down their concentration gradient, through a channel protein or carrier protein.

items.label: Pump protein
items.clue: An integral membrane protein that uses energy from ATP to change its shape and so transfer a specific particle from one side of the membrane to the other.

questions.stem: A lipid is found to form a continuous sheet-like bilayer when shaken with water. Which property must the lipid have?

options.text: It must be entirely hydrophobic, so that all of its molecules cluster together away from water.
It must be amphipathic, with a hydrophilic region and a hydrophobic region in each molecule.
It must be able to form covalent bonds with neighbouring lipid molecules in the sheet.
It must be acted on by an enzyme that assembles the molecules into the bilayer.

questions.stem: Which of these particles crosses a pure phospholipid bilayer, with no proteins present, least readily?

options.text: A carbon dioxide molecule, which is larger than a water molecule
An oxygen molecule, which needs a protein to cross the bilayer
A sodium ion, which is small but charged and hydrophilic
A water molecule, which is very small and also polar

questions.explanation: The hydrophobic core has very low permeability to hydrophilic particles, including ions and polar molecules. A charged sodium ion cannot enter the hydrocarbon core, so it has the lowest permeability of the four.

questions.stem: A cell is respiring rapidly, so its internal oxygen concentration is low. How do oxygen molecules enter the cell?

options.text: They diffuse through a channel protein that is specific for oxygen and opens when needed
They are moved in by a pump protein using ATP, because the cell needs oxygen urgently
They move in and out randomly until the concentrations are equal, then stop moving
They pass between the phospholipids by simple diffusion down their gradient

questions.stem: Which statement about membrane proteins is correct?

options.text: Integral proteins are embedded in one or both lipid layers, while peripheral proteins are attached to a surface.
Integral proteins all span the whole bilayer, while peripheral proteins are embedded in only one layer.
Integral and peripheral proteins are both transport proteins, differing only in the substance they carry.
Glycoproteins carry their carbohydrate on both faces of the membrane, so the two surfaces are identical.

questions.stem: Some cells lining the kidney tubules have large numbers of aquaporins in their plasma membranes. What is the effect of these aquaporins?

options.text: They pump water across the membrane against its gradient, using ATP energy.
They allow water to cross the membrane, which is otherwise impossible for the bilayer.
They greatly increase the rate at which water can cross the membrane by osmosis.
They let water move in the direction the cell needs, whatever the solute concentrations.

questions.stem: A potassium channel in a cell membrane is open. Which statement describes the movement of ions through it?

options.text: Potassium ions and any other ions of similar size diffuse through the open pore.
Potassium ions are moved through in whichever direction the cell requires.
Potassium ions are carried through using energy from the hydrolysis of ATP.
Potassium ions diffuse through, down their gradient, with no ATP used.

questions.explanation: A channel provides a hydrophilic route through the hydrophobic core for one specific ion. The ions move by facilitated diffusion, down their concentration gradient, and no energy from ATP is needed.

questions.stem: Which statement about glycoproteins in the plasma membrane is correct?

options.text: Their carbohydrate is on the cytoplasmic side and is respired when the cell lacks glucose.
Their carbohydrate projects from both faces of the membrane so that either face can be recognised.
Their carbohydrate is on the extracellular side and is used in cell recognition and adhesion.
They are transport proteins whose carbohydrate forms the channel through which sugars enter the cell.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly applies the term organelle as it is used in IB Biology?

options.text: The plasma membrane is an organelle, although it forms the boundary of the cytoplasm.
Ribosomes are not organelles, because they are not bounded by a membrane.
The cell wall is an organelle, because it is a labelled part with a function.
The cytoskeleton is an organelle, because it is a structure that moves organelles.

questions.explanation: An organelle is a discrete subunit of a cell adapted to a specific function. The plasma membrane is such a unit, controlling exchange with the surroundings, and the guide lists it with nuclei, vesicles and ribosomes as an organelle.

questions.stem: A gene from a eukaryote is inserted into a bacterium and is transcribed there. In the eukaryotic cell the mRNA from this gene would be modified before translation. What happens to the mRNA in the bacterium?

options.text: It is modified in the cytoplasm before ribosomes can bind it.
It is translated inside the nucleoid before it is released.
It is not translated, as bacterial ribosomes read the DNA.
It is translated at once, without any modification.

questions.explanation: In prokaryotes there is no nuclear membrane separating transcription from translation, so mRNA may immediately meet ribosomes and be translated, even while it is still being transcribed. Post-transcriptional modification is not possible.

questions.stem: In a human, a neuron and a liver cell are both descended by mitosis from the same zygote. What is the difference between them once they have differentiated?

options.text: They express different subsets of the same complete set of genes.
They have kept different sets of genes and discarded the rest.
They were set on different paths inside from fertilization.
They differ only until the body needs to swap them over.

questions.stem: Which pair of properties defines a stem cell?

options.text: Ability to divide whenever a tissue is damaged and to produce more cells of its own type.
Ability to switch from one specialized type to another whenever a tissue requires this.
Capacity to divide endlessly and ability to differentiate along different pathways.
Continuous division at all times, giving new cells whether or not they are needed.

questions.explanation: These are the two defining properties in the guide: a stem cell can divide endlessly, and it can differentiate along different pathways to give specialized cell types. Both are required.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes pluripotent stem cells from totipotent stem cells?

options.text: Pluripotent cells can form any cell type of the body but not extra-embryonic tissues such as the placenta.
Pluripotent and totipotent cells can both form every cell type, so the two terms are interchangeable.
Pluripotent cells are the stem cells found in adult tissues such as bone marrow and hair follicles.
Pluripotent cells appear only after birth, since all the cells of an embryo remain totipotent.

questions.stem: Which statement about voltage-gated sodium channels in the membrane of a neuron is correct?

options.text: They open in response to a change in membrane potential and allow sodium ions to diffuse down their gradient.
They open when acetylcholine binds to them and allow sodium ions to diffuse down their gradient.
They open in response to a change in membrane potential and pump sodium ions in using ATP.
They open whenever any small ion is present and allow it to pass through into the neuron.

questions.stem: What happens to the nuclear membrane during mitosis, and why?

options.text: It pinches into two so that each daughter nucleus keeps part of the original envelope.
It opens its pores wider so that the chromosomes can pass out into the cytoplasm.
It stays intact throughout, because the chromosomes can diffuse through its two bilayers.
It breaks into vesicles so that spindle microtubules can reach the chromosomes.

questions.explanation: Spindle microtubules form in the cytoplasm. The nuclear membrane breaks into vesicles during mitosis and meiosis so that the microtubules can attach to the chromosomes and move them; the envelope re-forms from vesicles around each daughter nucleus.

questions.stem: A vesicle from the Golgi apparatus carries a protein to the plasma membrane for secretion. What happens to the membrane of the vesicle when the protein is released?

options.text: It passes out through the plasma membrane and is lost from the cell.
It is broken down into phospholipids reused to build the next vesicle.
It stays joined to the Golgi apparatus as a channel for more protein.
It fuses with the plasma membrane and becomes part of it.

questions.explanation: In exocytosis the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing the contents outside the cell. The vesicle's phospholipids and proteins are added to the plasma membrane, which is also how the membrane of a growing cell is enlarged.
